#3576. GTA 6's strong and silent Jason was inspired by Steve McQueen and former Army Rangers, says Rockstar

If you've noticed that Grand Theft Auto 6's Jason Duval isn't much of a talker, that's by design, as his quiet nature was inspired by Steve McQueen and the studio's research into former Army Rangers.

Speaking to Destructoid over email, Rockstar's senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, explained that the team looked at classic couple-on-the-run films when it decided on GTA 6's story.

"When we decided we wanted to tell a story about a couple on the run, we looked at all the similar kinds of movies, and one of the ones that really stood out was Peckinpah's The Getaway," Humphries said. "Steve McQueen was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone. We wanted to see how close we could get to that with a game character, where so many of our protagonists have been the opposite."

That approach also fitted the studio's research into veterans. "This also resonated with the research we were doing around veterans and particularly former Army Rangers (in our world we call them Marauders)," Humphries continued. "These guys typically aren't running their mouths or reacting to something unless it's strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves."

Game writer Michael Wiafe said Florida's real-life crime stories were "an obvious starting point" for GTA 6's characters more broadly.

"From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either," Wiafe said. "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn't necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don't attempt to make excuses for them."

Fellow writer Elizabeth Gauvey-Kern added that while "the story takes some pretty heavy turns", Jason and Lucia's goal remains consistent. "So sharing their sense of determination, the focus on their goal, through all the highs and lows - that's what I hope people feel more than anything. You really want them to make it."

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day, not everyone is happy: some players have been review bombing its Metacritic user score over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

Just don't share any, uh, spicy in-game screenshots via PSN - we recently learned that a GTA 6 player was hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

The Big Bang Theory may be a popular and highly regarded sitcom on its own but, at this point, it’s also spawned multiple spinoffs that have cumulatively led to the formation of a franchise. Of course, the first offshoot from the Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady-created sitcom was Young Sheldon, which debuted in 2017. Aside from having tonal differences from Big Bang, the series also had a single-camera set-up as opposed to a multi-cam one with a live audience. I always wondered why that was the case and, now, I finally have my answer.

Young Sheldon is a prequel series focusing on the exploits of the titular Sheldon Cooper and his Texas-based family. The show received its share of love while it was on CBS, and that’s remained the case since it wrapped up its seven-season run in 2024. Obviously, the family sitcom works as is, considering how successful it’s been, but I still couldn’t help but wonder why the producer changed up the format from the parent series. To my surprise, Lorre addressed that during an interview with Channel 4, and the reason is quite practical:

It's more intimate. The pacing, obviously, is very different. The actors aren't having to hold for laughs. They're not playing to the proscenium. They're working with one another. You know, a four camera show is played like a theatrical presentation. They're playing to the audience, and it changes the tone and the pitch and the pacing.

So, apparently, Lorre, along with co-showrunners Steven Molaro and Steve Holland, sought a somewhat more personal vibe for this show that didn’t quite mesh with the breakneck pace of a multi-camera comedy. While I’m someone who has long enjoyed situation comedies that have live audiences, even I can understand the rationale here. There are just some stories that lend themselves better to the single camera format. And that’s not the only reason for Young Sheldon’s changing things up from its famous predecessor:

And also, we knew going in that we were going to be working with a cast of young children, and it seemed like the more appropriate way for them to get the best work, to do the best work, was in a closed setting where they had the time to develop these characters.

One Producer Gets Honest About Elon Musk’s Big Bang Theory And Young Sheldon Cameos

I’d imagine that for an actor of any age it can be a little daunting to act in front of a live audience, and doing so is also tedious. Based on Lorre’s sentiments, I imagine that was his thinking in regard to choosing the format for YS. Plenty of current and former child actors (including many still working today) have, of course, given excellent performances on multi-camera sitcoms. Still, I can definitely understand how working with young performers in a more controlled environment would be easier for them and the crew.

With the Big Bang franchise still pushing on, the producers have been varying up how those shows are presented. For example, the Young Sheldon spinoff, Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, has a live studio audience, and the series premiere even addresses that switch in a meta way. The IP’s latest entry, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, meanwhile is a single-camera show that’s heavy on visual effects (which Lorre had “no experience with”).

All in all, it seems that for each Big Bang-related show, Chuck Lorre and co. just want to go with the format that feels most appropriate. It’s honestly hard to argue with the choices they’ve made up to this point, considering the success of the series. Check out The Big Bang Theory, Young Sheldon and Stuart Fails to Save the Universe by streaming them with an HBO Max subscription. Also, Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage airs on Thursdays at 8 p.m. ET amid the 2026 TV schedule.

#3574. Kate Middleton Wore Matching Amethyst Necklace and Earrings for Her First Engagement in India

The Princess of Wales touched down in India this Monday for a whirlwind three-day visit to the country with her husband, Prince William.

The couple visited Mumbai for the sixth Earthshot Prize Summit, which took place on Tuesday. It marked the Waleses’ first joint overseas visit since Catherine’s cancer diagnosis.

The busy schedule of engagements kicked off with a game of gully cricket—an informal version of the game played on the street. For the occasion, the Princess of Wales struck a balance between polished and casual, opting for crisp white Alexander McQueen trousers, paired with a white top layered under a pistachio blazer by Veronica Beard.

The Princess of Wales debuted a pistachio blazer by Veronica Beard for the outing

The finishing touch? A matching set of green amethyst earrings and a drop necklace from one of Catherine’s favorite jewelry labels, Kiki McDonough. Catherine has at least 20 pairs of earrings from the jeweler, ranging from the blue topaz drops she wore to Royal Ascot to the green tourmaline, green amethyst and diamond earrings set in gold, designed specially for her to mark Princess Charlotte’s birth.

The apple green amethysts, which she wore in Mumbai, are among the lesser-seen designs in her collection but proved the perfect accessory for this first engagement.

While in Mumbai, the prince’s program focused on The Earthshot Prize and its mission to accelerate solutions to the world’s most pressing environmental challenges. The princess joined the prince for a number of engagements during the visit.

The Prince and Princess of Wales in Mumbai on Monday

During their time in Mumbai, the prince and princess also celebrated several of the deep cultural connections between the United Kingdom and India: cricket, fashion, and cinema.

Beginning with an engagement focused on the uniquely Indian passion of gully cricket andconcluding with a visit to the heart of Mumbai’s film industry, their royal highnessescelebrated the creativity, talent, and cultural influence that continue to shape modern India andstrengthen ties between the two countries.

The highlight of the visit was the Earthshot Prize ceremony on Tuesday, November 17. Five Earthshot leaders were given 1 million euros (about $1.1 million USD) to accelerate the impact of their innovative solutions. Mumbai made perfect sense as the host city; India is home to more Earthshot Prize winners and finalists than any other country.

The Princess of Wales looked elegant in a lime green blazer layered over an all-white ensemble

Since founding the prize in 2020, Prince William has attended all of the awards ceremonies: in London, Boston, Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro. Catherine joined the prince in London in 2021 and again in Boston the following year, but has missed recent editions in the further corners of the globe. This was partly due to the princess’s restricted work schedule while she underwent treatment for cancer and spent time in recovery.

It marked a return to the country for Prince William and Kate, who carried out a state visit in April 2016. The week-long tour saw the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge explore Mumbai, New Delhi, Assam, and Bhutan, racking up a total of 22 engagements that saw them try their hand at cricket, meet Bollywood stars and royalty, and champion charitable causes close to their hearts.

It was one of four overseas trips taken by the couple that year. Although William and Kate still travel, it is with far less frequency as the couple prioritizes a stable family life. Their last major overseas tour was to the Caribbean in 2022.

#3573. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Is in a Battle for His Own Survival at the Pentagon

The day after the midterm elections, President Donald Trump met with Susie Wiles in the Oval Office. He asked his chief of staff whether she believed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth would survive the impeachment attempt that would soon be launched by a member of his own party.

Hegseth was in a precarious position. He had been among the most aggressive champions of the war with Iran, widely seen as the policy most responsible for the shellacking Republicans had taken the night before. Wiles remained officially supportive of Hegseth throughout her time in the White House, but she had harbored concerns about the secretary from the start. She did not believe he was forthright about his skeletons during a rocky confirmation process, and she considered the subsequent Signalgate scandal an amateurish disaster.

In the Wednesday meeting, according to a senior White House official, Wiles made clear that the war, the uncertainty of its next steps, and the inflation it had fueled all contributed to the midterms debacle. She offered her resignation, but Trump declined. On Thursday night, in a contentious meeting in the Oval Office, she offered to resign again. Trump announced the next day that Wiles would leave the White House for his outside political operation.

Hegseth’s fate was still uncertain. A deeply unpopular figure among the American public, presiding over an even more unpopular war, he faced an impeachment push led by Representative Thomas Massie. “He is just failing,” said Republican senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina—who voted to confirm Hegseth at the start of Trump’s term—in an interview with Vanity Fair. “In the same way that Kristi Noem failed at Homeland Security, he simply doesn’t have the instincts or the prior experience as an executive that is necessary for this particular role.”

The secretary of defense has now embarked on a campaign to save his job, and Stephen Miller’s elevation to replace Wiles as Trump’s chief of staff has helped to ensure a reprieve. Trump has so far backed Hegseth publicly, and last week, House Republicans blocked the impeachment effort. “Pete is a fighter,” the White House official explained. “Trump likes fighters.” And there are other reasons to keep him in place, the official said: Confirming a replacement will not be easy, particularly when Democrats take control of Congress, and ousting Hegseth would signal an admission that at this point, Trump’s war is a failure.

It was the president’s taste for staffers out of central casting that helped put Hegseth—a weekend morning television host with no experience in government, but with the square jaw of an Army Wives extra—in charge of the Department of Defense. He has relied on his talents before the cameras, and a team of advisers attuned to the production of his persona, to both keep his job and sell Trump on aggressive military action from the Pacific to the Persian Gulf. His survival has depended in part on his ability to project strength—not to the public, or to the rank-and-file, but to the president.

“In just under two years, Secretary Hegseth has worked side-by-side with President Trump to restore American power on the world stage, build the strongest military in generations, and instill a warrior ethos at the Pentagon,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement. “President Trump and Secretary Hegseth have taken bold, necessary action to deny the Iranian regime the ability to develop a nuclear weapon, bring narco-terrorist Nicolas Maduro to American justice, and defend our homeland from dangerous terrorists and cartels—saving American lives.”

“They will stand behind him in the short term,” said a second senior administration official. And yet, “He is a cost. He’s constantly requiring people to spend political capital on him. The White House is constantly having to come in and save him. The question is, at what point is it too much of a cost to the president?”

The morning after Hegseth survived the impeachment attempt, he attended a Veterans Day ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Hegseth was joined at the sacred memorial by his closest aides: Jennifer Hegseth, his third wife and a former Fox News producer who serves as an informal but influential adviser; his chief of staff Ricky Buria, a Marine Corps veteran who followed an unusual path into the top brass; and Tami Radabaugh, another former Fox News producer whom Hegseth hired as a senior adviser.

As the group posed for photos at the Tomb, they chatted and laughed loudly. A US Army sentinel guarding the memorial turned to the group and shouted out a reprimand: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” After video of the moment made for embarrassing headlines, Hegseth awarded the soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal and posed alongside several Army officers for a photoshoot that was posted on his social media accounts. The Pentagon did not elaborate on why a soldier was awarded a medal for an act as pedestrian as scolding noisy attendees at a memorial. “Hegseth would not have given him that award had the incident not been on TV,” said a former senior defense official.

The small group of advisers beside Hegseth has helped the secretary weather a series of scandals in his two years as defense secretary using stage-managed displays of toughness. “He’s a cross between a carnival barker and a personal trainer,” said John Ullyot, who served as chief Pentagon spokesperson and senior adviser to Hegseth until he left the department last year. A loyal Trump backer, Ullyot initially supported Hegseth’s calls to restore standards and excise identity politics from the military. He has since emerged as a fierce public critic and now believes Hegseth should resign.

In his new book, The President Deserves Better, Ullyot describes a secretary of defense fixated on self-promotion and content creation. Jennifer plays an instrumental role in those efforts, directing the secretary’s social media and a small battalion of accounts that support him online. “It was as if she was producing him in his role as Secretary,” Ullyot writes. She has helped produce—and starred in—dramatic videos of Hegseth posted by the Pentagon’s official social media accounts. “Her entire job is to make his image,” one source told Vanity Fair.

House Republican Thomas Massie, who brought the articles of impeachment against Hegseth last week, argued the bombing was “the result of systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians.”

Her role extended well beyond production, alarming senior officials in the Department of Defense. She interviewed candidates for Pentagon roles. She attended sensitive bilateral meetings with foreign officials. She was included in Signal chats that discussed the war plans for the Houthi operation in Yemen. The former defense official said they warned Hegseth about his wife’s involvement in Pentagon affairs. “She did not have a fucking clearance,” they said. “She shouldn’t be privy to this shit.”

Hegseth himself seemed too smitten to care. He covered the walls of his office, as well as other meeting rooms and corridors throughout the Pentagon, with large photos of himself and his wife. When The New York Times examined Jennifer’s influence at the department over the summer, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the former cable news producer “an accomplished leader.” He added that the Pentagon “not only welcomes her current leadership but actively plans to involve her even more deeply in the future.” Politico later reported that while advising the secretary of defense, Jennifer was being paid for consulting work by Watchtower Strategies, a Washington lobbying shop that counts Lockheed Martin as a client.

She wasn’t the only Fox News producer at the Pentagon. Hegseth also gave Radabaugh—a former producer on Fox & Friends Weekend with no government experience—broad authority over department affairs, I’m told. Radabaugh made sure that glamorous photos and videos of Hegseth were published online promptly, sometimes scolding aides for taking too long to post. In the first few months of Hegseth’s tenure, she ordered Ullyot to turn a room just off the briefing room into a makeup studio.

“This was ridiculous. I said not only no, but hell no,” Ullyot writes. He warned that news of the makeup studio would leak. “How exactly did a makeup studio fit into the warrior ethos?”

In response to a detailed list of questions, Pentagon spokesman Joel Valdez declined to answer many of them but emailed a lengthy statement criticizing Ullyot. “There is no ‘makeup studio’ in the Pentagon, and it never existed,” Valdez said, going on to call Ullyot “a skinwalker,” a “sour puss coward,” and “generally a stupid person” who left “his job in disgrace.” (According to information reviewed by Vanity Fair, Hegseth praised Ullyot after his departure from the Pentagon and offered to recommend him to Susie Wiles, then Trump’s chief of staff.)

“I volunteered to help stand up the Secretary’s press operation for a few months at the start of his term,” Ullyot told Vanity Fair in response. “I left as planned, and the Secretary thanked me for my work. My record over more than 30 years, including as a senior spokesman in the Senate and in the Trump White House, speaks for itself.”

Hegseth was bullish on the war with Iran from the start. “There weren’t any real cheerleaders for the war in the cabinet outside of Pete Hegseth,” said the second official. “It was Pete and [US Ambassador to Israel] Mike Huckabee.”

Soon after his confirmation, Hegseth moved to increase his powers and consolidate control over the Pentagon. He ousted generals and subjected senior staff to polygraph tests to weed out leakers, a crusade that resulted in the abrupt firings of top officials that demoralized staff. He tapped Tim Parlatore, his personal lawyer, as a special adviser and charged him with overseeing leak investigations. Parlatore continued to run his own private practice as a criminal defense attorney, and Politico reported this week that while serving as Hegseth’s top adviser, he is representing the son of a Libyan warlord accused of extrajudicial killings and torture.

In keeping with the president’s broad campaign for retribution, Hegseth ordered an investigation into retired Joint Chiefs Chairman General Mark Milley, who had clashed with Trump during his first term, and stripped the four-star general of his security detail. The Pentagon is now working on a new report on the 2021 Kabul Airport attack, during which 13 American soldiers and 170 Afghan civilians were killed in a suicide bombing during the withdrawal from Afghanistan. At the time, Milley served as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The new assessment, one source familiar with the investigation said, is expected by the end of the month and is intended to serve as a predicate to strip Milley of his four-star rank.

Hegseth waged a parallel war on the press, starting with an attempt to ban NBC News correspondent Courtney Kube from the Pentagon. In a meeting with his advisers, Ullyot writes, Hegseth explained that he and his wife Jennifer were “angry” at Kube for how much she covered his turbulent confirmation process before Congress. “I thought this was loony tunes,” Ullyot writes. One source told me that after NBC News was kicked out of its Pentagon office, Hegseth aides took a full-length mirror from the vacated room and installed it in his makeup studio.

As Hegseth purged senior officials, he grew closer to Buria. The relationship was confounding to many inside the building: Hegseth has pushed to cleanse the Pentagon of ideological diversity, yet he elevated Buria, a holdover from the Biden administration who had previously donated to Democrats. But Buria had earned the trust of Jennifer. When explaining to advisers why he was elevated, Hegseth said he prayed about the decision with his wife. “And you know what? Jen says he’s really good with the kids,” Hegseth told them.

Buria was by Hegseth’s side throughout the Signalgate scandal, which, according to several administration officials, was a turning point for the secretary. “Every problem he is having in one way or another goes back to Signalgate,” the second Trump official said. “His extremely hostile relations with the press, his paranoia, his firing of certain people, denied promotions to generals. It was all around paranoia related to Signalgate.”

“There’s two versions of Hegseth,” said a second former defense official. “There is the pre-Signalgate version and the post-Signalgate version. It’s like Jekyll and Hyde. He was Dr. Jekyll until around Signalgate, and he’s been Mr. Hyde ever since. He’s just not making good decisions.”

It was an almost unbelievable incident: Hegseth shared war plans for a bombing campaign against the Houthis in Yemen on at least two Signal group chats, including one that inadvertently included Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor in chief of The Atlantic.

This was the first major military engagement of Hegseth’s tenure, but he chose to survey the operation with Buria from a temporary secure facility at his Fort McNair home rather than make the short trip to the Pentagon or the White House Situation Room. The decision alarmed some at the Pentagon. “It’s your first major military operation,” said the second senior Trump official. “Why would you monitor it from your shitty SCIF in your basement? Why not go 10 minutes to the Pentagon where you have the joint staff?”

“You would think with kinetic operations going on in the Middle East that could have dramatic consequences for service members, that he’d be in the office,” Tillis said.

Trump has so far backed Hegseth publicly, and last week, House Republicans blocked the impeachment effort. “Pete is a fighter,” the White House official explained. “Trump likes fighters.”

During Hegseth’s confirmation process, allegations of heavy drinking concerned Republican lawmakers he needed to vote in favor of his nomination. At the time, several Republican senators said he promised them he would stop boozing if confirmed. He affirmed this pledge publicly: “This is the biggest deployment of my life,” he told Megyn Kelly in a 2024 interview, “and there won’t be a drop of alcohol on my lips while I’m doing it.”

Whether or not Hegseth has actually quit drinking continues to be a source of palace intrigue. One official recalled watching Hegseth drink what the secretary suggested were two cocktails—though the official conceded he hadn’t seen the drinks poured, and raised a theory that Hegseth might have been testing whether he would leak the incident to the press. “This was at a time of peak paranoia,” the official said.

Buria was known to drink on official trips; the official recalled Hegseth’s aide handing out shots to passengers on a US government jet during a Pentagon junket. Two other officials said Buria would often brag about drinking with Hegseth, including on an official trip to Panama in 2025. The New York Post later reported that Buria had made up a story about him and Hegseth donning disguises to go out and drink, all in an effort to weed out leakers. One of the officials told me they believed the leak claim was Buria’s retroactive effort to cover up that he was boasting about drinking with the secretary.

“The drinking is what they’re really afraid of,” the second official said. When asked directly if Hegseth continued drinking as secretary, a Defense Department spokesperson who declined to be named said in a statement: “No, the Secretary has kept his promise that he made during his confirmation hearings and has not drank since becoming Secretary of War.”

Jennifer and Pete Hegseth have forged a close relationship with Stephen Miller and his wife Katie, their neighbors on a placid and heavily fortified army base south of the White House. Hegseth’s temporary salvation comes thanks in part to support from Miller, who values his deference to Trump. “Stephen doesn’t like all the Liberace shit, the cucaracha shit,” said the first former official. “Pete right now is fresh out of friends, and misery loves company. But don’t get it twisted. At any moment, at any second, Stephen will cut Pete’s throat.”

The secretary of defense has made few friends in Washington. One source recalled attending a holiday party stocked with members of the administration during which Hegseth spent much of his time alone in the corner of the room. “Even Kash Patel had people coming up to him to talk,” the source said. “Pete was alone and isolated. He looked depressed. And this was before the Iran war. His stock has not gone up since then.”

Hegseth has channeled much of his effort into appealing to an audience of one, telling advisers he only cares about Trump’s opinion. “The one thing he’s been successful at, and I think it’s the only thing, is flattering Donald Trump constantly,” the former official said.

The purpose of this flattery campaign extends beyond keeping his current job. In private, Hegseth has confided in several officials about his ambitions to run for president. This jockeying has exacerbated tensions with Vice President JD Vance. The relationship was already strained by Vance’s private opposition to the Iran war, and it deteriorated significantly after the vice president’s close friend, Dan Driscoll, was pushed out of his position as Army Secretary in August following months of friction with Hegseth.

When explaining to advisers why Buria was elevated, Hegseth said he prayed about the decision with his wife. “And you know what? Jen says he’s really good with the kids,” Hegseth told them.

“Secretary Hegseth and Vice President Vance share an outstanding working relationship grounded in deep mutual respect and alignment,” Parnell said in a statement to Vanity Fair.

Jennifer has worked in tandem with her husband to push allies on social media and in the press to promote the idea of a presidential run. “She wants to be first lady,” the former official said of Jennifer. “She wants to be Hillary.” After the midterms, online influencers whom Hegseth hired earlier this year to work as special government employees at the Pentagon began pitching Hegseth for president. These influencers were nominally hired to promote Hegseth’s efforts to bring war colleges in line with the “warrior ethos,” but in reality they coordinated with Jennifer and Radabaugh on “shitposting,” the second official said. Earlier this month, they rallied to Hegseth’s defense as he came under fire for the Republican ballot box-bloodbath, posting action shots of the secretary with the caption: “STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC.”

These influencers often attack journalists who cover the Pentagon. In response to a recent story by Politico’s Daniel Lippman, an active-duty Army officer known as InfantryDort on social media—whom Hegseth hired as one of these shadow spokespeople—posted: “I expect you all to ratio the fuck out of this retard and in short order. Daniel Lippman remains absolute journalistic filth.” A Politico spokesperson responded: “Daniel is one of Washington’s best-sourced reporters, and we’re lucky to have him at POLITICO.”

When Democrats take control of Congress, they are expected to focus much of their oversight on Hegseth, including the scandals from his personal life. The subjects broached in his contentious confirmation hearings—including an affidavit signed by his former sister-in-law alleging abuse against his second wife—are likely to be relitigated. (His second wife denied that she was physically abused.)

“Is that going to be good for the president?” Tillis asked. “His entire confirmation will be re-prosecuted. That affidavit will get a lot of attention. Family members will most likely be subpoenaed. Does he really want to go through that at a personal level, and at the same time be such a massive disruption for the leader of the most lethal, complex organization in American government? Is this about Pete, or is this about America’s defense? I don’t know how any objective person can say that the value that he brings is greater than that distraction and the cost of him remaining in place.”

“If he had any dignity, he would resign and allow the president to appoint a replacement in the lame duck session,” said the first official. “But he doesn’t.”

Hegseth’s ability to project confidence is not confined to the cameras. He was bullish on the war with Iran from the start. “There weren’t any real cheerleaders for the war in the cabinet outside of Pete Hegseth,” said the second official. “It was Pete and [US Ambassador to Israel] Mike Huckabee.” In late December 2025, Hegseth met with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Four Seasons in Palm Beach shortly before Netanyahu ventured to Mar-a-Lago to make the case for fresh strikes on Iran. By February, Netanyahu was pushing Trump to join Israel in a full-blown war to topple the Iranian regime.

Hegseth was all-in, his confidence buoyed by the success of Operation Midnight Hammer—a series of strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025—and the raid to abduct Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro. His allies in the administration point to these operations, as well as a post-pandemic surge in military recruitment numbers, as his major successes in the job.

But multiple officials who spoke with Vanity Fair said they believed that when briefing Trump, Hegseth understated the risks of war with Iran from the beginning and went on to overstate its successes as the conflict dragged on. “Pete gave the rosiest picture in the world,” said the first former official. During early discussions about potentially launching the war, the official said they were struck by how quickly Hegseth started speaking about the operation as a “foregone conclusion.”

“Leading up into the war, he presented, along with [Central Command Commander Admiral] Brad Cooper, overly optimistic projections of what the air campaign could achieve,” said the second administration official. “This is how the president got this idea that it could be done in a matter of two to three weeks.”

Hegseth ran against Democrat U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar in 2012.

Tillis, for his part, said that he did not believe Hegseth was forthright with Trump about the war. “He planned the good, bright, shiny stuff that was Epic Fury, but clearly did not brief the president on things that anybody that’s had any experience in the Middle East knows,” Tillis added. “The first thing that goes is the Strait of Hormuz.”

“Secretary Hegseth and Pentagon leadership consistently provide the President with the complete, unvarnished picture so he can make the best choices for America’s security and success,” Parnell said in a statement.

On the first day of the war, a missile struck the Minab elementary school in southern Iran, killing more than 150 people, the majority of them children. The US military has thus far refused to publicly admit responsibility for the strike, despite a preliminary military investigation concluding within days of the strike that a US missile struck the school. Before the attack, Hegseth gutted the Pentagon program aimed at reducing civilian harm during military operations, ProPublica reported in March. House Republican Thomas Massie, who brought the articles of impeachment against Hegseth last week, argued the bombing was “the result of systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians.”

Massie cast the strike as a consequence of Hegseth’s oft-repeated mantra: “Maximum lethality, not tepid legality.”

As the war went on, officials said, Hegseth continued to trumpet its successes, showing the president what one official described as “hype videos” depicting strikes on missile launchers, Iranian ships, and old aircraft. Hegseth told Trump “that the majority of Iran’s missile capabilities and the majority of Iran’s Air Force was destroyed,” the official said, even though US intelligence “showed that wasn’t the case, and that the majority of Iran’s missiles and missile launchers by the end of the major combat phase of the war were still intact.”

“He creates an echo chamber in the press corps so that he can get only nice questions or do made-for-TV stuff,” said Senator Tillis.

Hegseth also worked behind the scenes to promote positive media coverage of the war. He briefed Fox News hosts whom he remained friendly with on the war’s progress and encouraged them to present a positive picture on air. But Hegseth himself has made little effort to explain or defend the war to Americans. Even as the war has become a political debacle for the administration, he remains bullish on escalation. “Pete is the only one who wants to restart strikes,” the first official said.

We were all sitting in our assigned seats waiting for the performance to start when a security official walked into the Pentagon briefing room to make an announcement. Hegseth had not held a Pentagon press briefing since May. Now, facing an impeachment effort from a member of his own party, he came before the cameras. “If anyone gets out of line today, you’re going to be physically removed,” the official said. “Is that clear?”

“Sense of decorum,” the official said apologetically. “Just be professional.”

The official said he was just relaying orders from Hegseth’s office. A few minutes later, Joel Valdez, the press aide, walked out and asked if anyone was confused. Everyone was. “I could tell you off the record?” he said. No, the reporters replied. “Do you want to hear it off the record?” No, they said again.

Valdez looked down at his shoes and then walked out of the room without saying another word. “In my 30 years in DC, I have never heard that,” said a cameraman. “This is crazytown.”

At 8 a.m. sharp, Hegseth walked out wearing a loud plaid suit, a striped tie, and an American flag pocket square. The timing is no coincidence; officials said Hegseth schedules briefings in the 8 a.m. hour because Trump is known to watch Fox News at that time.

The secretary of defense began reading his speech from a stack of papers on the podium. From my assigned seat in the back row, I felt as if I were watching an interpretive dance. The choreography of Hegseth’s hand movements and facial expressions was as slick as his hair, which was gelled into a stiff meringue that moved in unison with his tanned face.

Hegseth punctuated a line about President Trump’s “decisive” leadership with a clenched fist thrust downward. The word “overseeing” was expressed with a slow swipe of the hand over an imaginary stretch of purview. As Hegseth recalled the glories of the Maduro operation—and, parenthetically, his part in directing them—he dismissed criticism of the raid by leaning into the microphone, shaking his head from side to side and wiggling his eyebrows: “It wasn’t”—dramatic pause for eyebrow wiggle—“a kidnapping.”

Hegseth's presser had a pantomime quality.

The briefing itself exuded little of the confidence Hegseth sought to signal before the cameras. He took seven questions in total, sticking to friendly reporters in the front rows who had signed a pledge in September 2025 to not report “unauthorized information” from the Pentagon. One of them, a representative of Real America’s Voice, asked “what message” is sent to America’s allies when “our own politicians don’t support taking out the narco traffickers that kill their own constituents?” It wasn’t so much a question as a warm bath. Some in the room, visibly frustrated by the waste of time, rolled their eyes. Others shouted questions from the back about Iran and impeachment. Hegseth refused to look at them.

“He creates an echo chamber in the press corps so that he can get only nice questions or do made-for-TV stuff,” said Tillis, who also decried Hegseth for filming a slick video of himself outside the Department of Defense making the case for why he should not be impeached: “He demonstrated more impulsiveness by using taxpayer dollars to defend himself against impeachment.”

In his remarks before the press, Hegseth framed the effort to remove him as an attack on the troops. “If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me,” he said, jabbing a finger into his chest. But the impeachment targeted Hegseth, not “the warriors.” We had assembled to hear Pete make the case for Pete. Indeed, he had not held a press briefing when a Navy commander died in a helicopter crash on July 1, or when three US soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a base in Jordan on July 17. What brought him back before the cameras was not the ongoing war in the Middle East but his own fight to save his career here in Washington.

The performance earned a rave review from the one viewer who mattered. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Early on in Hegseth’s tenure, he confided in advisers about his “biggest fear” as he took on the mighty responsibility of leading the Department of Defense, the first former official told me: “Being fired and embarrassed.” For now, Trump is standing by his secretary. He always is, until he isn’t. When asked just before the midterms whether Wiles would remain on as his chief of staff, Trump said there was “zero chance” he’d replace her. Three weeks later, she was out.

#3572. 5 Of The Best Sci-Fi Movies From This Century Are All Streaming In The Same Place

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

We've gotten some truly great sci-fi movies in the first quarter of this century, and I realized recently that five of the absolute best ones are all streaming in the same place. Whether its characters are traveling through space, trying to solve a mystery or trapped in a time loop, each of the movies I'm about to talk about are must-sees, and more importantly, must-see again and again.

All five of the movies on this list came out this century, and all of them can be streamed with a Paramount+ subscription. If you don't have one of those, there's a deal going on right now that you might want to check out.

Paramount+ is just $2.99 a month for the first two months right now for the holidays

The deal extends to both the Essential plan (normally $8.99 a month) and the ad-free Premium option ($13.99 a month). With plenty of great movies -- including sci-fi movies and TV shows  -- there's no shortage of great things to watch. That's not even scratching the surface of everything Paramount+ has to offer, either. Available now through November 30.

And with that, let's get on to the list of five of the best sci-fi movies from this century, all of which are streaming on Paramount+.

Christopher Nolan's epic movie sees Matthew McConaughey leaving his family behind to help an astronaut crew search for a new planet for mankind when Earth becomes uninhabitable. For a movie that's nearly three hours, Interstellar still manages to pace itself perfectly, while also balancing great character arcs, spectacular sci-fi visuals, a complex plot and a suspenseful build-up right to the end. Also, with actors like McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Michael Caine, Jessica Chastain and John Lithgow, the cast is sensational.

Amy Adams and Jeremy Renner star as two people brought in to try to translate the language of aliens who've recently invaded the planet. The words "intense," "emotional," "dramatic," and "spectacular" don't feel big enough to describe Denis Villeneuve's movie. Not only is Arrival one of the best sci-fi movies of all time, but it's one of my all-time favorite films, period. Years later, I still think about the ending of this movie.

Not to state the obvious, but sci-fi movies don't get nearly enough Academy Awards recognition. Gravity, fortunately, is a bit of an exception. Alfonso Cuarón's outstanding sci-fi thriller starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney had us all on the edge of our seats in theaters, and then again on Oscar night after it received 10 nominations (it missed Best Picture, but did win several other categories, including Director). This story of survival follows two astronauts trying to get back to Earth after a disaster strikes their shuttle. In addition to its great performances, Gravity also has some truly astounding special effects.

One of two Tom Cruise sci-fi movies on this list (and one of three mentioned), Steven Spielberg's Minority Report is set in a future where a metropolitan police department uses a predictive system involving psychics and technology to anticipate and prevent crime before it happens, detaining the murderers before they actually commit their crime. Cruise's character is a detective who pursues the would-be criminals, but ends up being pursued himself when the precogs predict he's about to commit a murder. There's action, mystery, and a lot of cool, futuristic technology in this one.

While most of the movies on this list come with a rather serious tone, I'd be remiss if I excluded Edge of Tomorrow just because it's full of alien battle chaos. Doug Liman's action-sci-fi movie is very much a popcorn flick, but in the best possible way. Tom Cruise plays a military officer who's forced into combat during a war waged on an invading species. When he finds himself stuck in a time loop, which resets the day every time he dies (and that happens a lot), he partners with Emily Blunt's character to try to find a way through it. It's exciting, full of action and big alien war scenes. It's even a bit funny at times.

Of course, if you want to make a Tom Cruise sci-fi trilogy out of your day, you can do just that, as Paramount+ also has Spielberg's War of the Worlds available streaming. While many would agree that Amazon's recent book-to-screen adaptation of H.G. Wells' sci-fi classic is not good, the 2005 movie starring Cruise and Dakota Fanning holds up rather nicely.

Kelly put her life-long love of movies, TV and books to greater use when she joined CinemaBlend as a freelance TV news writer in 2006, and went on to serve as the site’s TV Editor before joining the staff full-time in 2011 and moving over to other roles at the site. At present, she’s an Assistant Managing Editor who spends much of her time brainstorming and editing features, analyzing site data, working with writers and editors on content planning and the workflow, and obsessing over the best movies and TV shows. She graduated from SUNY Cortland with BA in Communication Studies and a minor in Cinema Studies. When she isn't working, she's probably thinking about work, or reading (or listening to a book), and making sure her cats are living their absolute best feline lives.

#3571. Joe Biden Has a Lot of Unknown Unknowns

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Good afternoon from Washington, where Party Animals has not forgotten the 5 a.m. wake-up required last Tuesday to attend Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first Pentagon press conference in six months. This was a peculiar one, arranged so Hegseth could brief the public on his own personal battle for career survival.

The briefing kicked off at 8 a.m., but the press had to be at the Pentagon by 6 a.m. for an extensive security screening. I’d like to think that this cruel early start was a consequence of Hegseth’s self-proclaimed sobriety. What kind of drunk drags his sorry carcass before a crowd of jackals before noon? Not any I know.

But sources I spoke with for a new piece on Hegseth’s war inside the Pentagon told me there was a more Machiavellian motivation for the presser: Donald Trump loves to watch Fox & Friends at 8 a.m. And sure enough, soon after the conclusion of Hegseth’s performance, its intended audience of one offered a review on Truth Social.

Read on for my investigation into Hegseth’s turbulent tenure at the top of the Department of Defense, and what it means for his survival as Democrats take control of Congress in January.

The reviews are in for Joe Biden’s new book, Promise Me, America. The Atlantic calls the book “unrepentant.” The New York Times calls it a 400-page “cover letter.” The former president offers the fantastical opinion that he should have stayed in the race in 2024 and faced Trump, quite a position to maintain given he couldn’t voice his own audiobook and limited his press appearances for the release to a soft-focus People magazine story (his publisher did not respond to Party Animals’ multiple requests for an interview). According to the reviews, the former president dedicates scant attention to one of the biggest debacles of his presidency, the war in Gaza, which he abetted thanks to near-unwavering support for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu as 2,000-pound bombs rained down on the densely packed enclave, killing more than 70,000 people. As president, Biden publicly questioned the death toll numbers. “Too many innocent Palestinians were killed,” he now writes, as if possessed by the passive-voice ghost of Donald Rumsfeld. Mistakes were made, indeed. In contrast with his remarkably clinical view of dead Gazans, he writes movingly about his friendship with Netanyahu, recalling his farewell to the prime minister days before leaving the White House: “I still love you, pal.”

Just five months ago, Elon Musk was promoting a movie in which a gunman goes on a mass murder rampage targeting supporters of immigration. That this was barely noticed is a sign of just how extreme Musk’s rhetoric has become over the years, as he devolved Xeet by Xeet into the online equivalent of a bum who yells at strangers on the street about race science. Then the midterms happened. After blowing nearly $500 million in an effort to get Republicans elected and falling short in key races, particularly in Texas, the octocentibillionaire seems to be seeking some kind of public rehabilitation. In a virtual appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin that he is “not MAGA”—despite the many photos of Elon wearing a certain conspicuous hat—and that he is actually “a moderate.” Don’t take the hat’s word for it, though, here’s Musk on the record in October 2024: “I’m not just MAGA, I’m Dark MAGA.” Ah, well, nevertheless. He expressed hope for incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, and said he felt “foolish” for blowing so many millions to achieve very little. What’s the over/under on how long Moderate Elon will last?

Miller and Marco: The Wall Street Journal has a great report on the close relationship between Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio, who have forged an unlikely alliance despite their past clashes over policy like immigration. It’s a revealing look at how Rubio’s Republican Party lost to Miller’s Republican Party, and how Rubio then jettisoned his entire worldview to join the winning team.

Trump of Wall Street: The Washington Post reports that Trump’s financial disclosure revealed he held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August. That’s considerably higher than the $615,000 to $1.3 million he held at the end of 2024.

French, Toast: No one should know who “Bo” French is. No one really did until the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commission went viral for complaining about a group of college kids celebrating a touchdown at a University of Texas football game. (Some of the kids were not white; French objected to this). He became whatever the opposite of a sensation is and ended up losing his election to a Democrat. Now Politico reports French has taken another blow: River Crest Country Club, the Fort Worth members institution he frequented, has kicked him out.

Garcia’s Hit List: Robert Garcia, the House Democrat who is expected to lead the Oversight Committee in the new Congress, has begun mapping out his targets. Per The Atlantic: “Garcia this morning sent a dozen letters to high-ranking Trump-administration officials and members of the president’s family, providing the clearest signal yet of which topics—and which people—will likely face the greatest scrutiny once Democrats take control of the House.”

Oversight O’clock: New York Magazine’s Ben Terris went deep on the new era of Democratic oversight, everything from the war with Iran to Trump’s big beautiful ballroom.

No Longer Satire: Read Joe Bernstein, writing for The New York Times Magazine, on how America is becoming more and more like Grand Theft Auto.

Bye-Bye Boebert: Annie Karni writes for The New York Times about the rise and fall of the MAGA Mean Girl Caucus, as Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert, and Nancy Mace all exit Congress.

#3570. Here's What We Know About Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 Sales

Gone are the days when holiday sales had a firm beginning and end. These days, if you're not scouring the internet weeks before the actual date of the event, you will miss out on deals. Black Friday is no exception. Amazon released its official Black Friday and Cyber Monday plans for its sale, but there's plenty that's discounted already, many reaching or matching their lowest price ever.

Amazon is treating Black Friday and Cyber Monday like one long sale. The official sale kicks off at 12:01 a.m. PST on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 30.

Yes, you will need to be a Prime Member to shop the exclusive sales during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Prime membership starts at $14.99 per month. While only you can decide if buying a yearly Prime membership is worth it for you, remember you can always sign up and then cancel your Prime membership once the sale is over: Amazon offers a free 30-day trial, so you can shop during both Black Friday and Cyber Monday before canceling without being charged. Here's how to sign up for a Prime account and all of the benefits that come with it.

This year, Amazon says you can expect "millions" of deals across categories like electronics, beauty, fashion, toys, home, and more from brands like Medicube, Le Creuset, HP, Google, and Stanley. There will also be limited-time deals of up to 60% off that will drop at midnight and 8 a.m. PST on both Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Here are some other deals Amazon says you can expect:

As stated already, just because the sale hasn't officially started, that doesn't mean you can't find great deals. You can follow all of our Black Friday coverage here. Here are some of the best deals we've found so far:

As far as volume, Amazon will usually beat Walmart and Best Buy in most cases, but most flagship products will likely be the same price in all three retailers. However, don't sleep on Walmart or Best Buy. There are usually a couple of surprising deals that beat Amazon (although Amazon usually matches the deal eventually).

The other major retailers doing sales are Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Best Buy is offering one of the largest Cyber Week sales, with new deals available every Friday. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

If this will be your first Black Friday shopping at Amazon, there are some basic things you need to know about Amazon sales:

You can share your Prime membership with family members using Amazon Family.

You can set price alerts for products you want, and your Alexa devices can notify you when they go on sale.

There are usually some invite-only deals that you can sign up for.

But if you only take one bit of advice for shopping on Amazon, let it be this one: Don't buy anything you weren't going to buy anyway. A good way to make sure you do this is by making a list of the products you do want, and only having eyes for those.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that you're less likely to see throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech.

#3569. GTA 6 Is Finally Here, So Come Watch Us Make Terrible Decisions In Vice City

In just a few short hours, the years-long wait for Grand Theft Auto 6 will finally be over. Maybe you're planning to hop on later today to start playing; maybe you've got a long weekend planned for the game. And maybe you should see exactly what you're in for, with the GameSpot video team livestream. Much of the conversation around Saturday Night Live last season was about Ashley Padilla. In just her sophomore turn, the comedian emerged as a clear breakout star and was the subject of numerous positive articles and think pieces about how she was becoming the face of the show. There was even a fair bit of outrage about the fact that she wasn’t promoted from featured player to full cast member mid-season. Most SNL fans, myself included, assumed Lorne Michaels and the writers would double down and fully build around her this season, potentially at the expense of other cast members, but six episodes in, the numbers are telling a different story.

Ashley Padilla is clearly still a focal point and core pillar of what Saturday Night Live is trying to do in Season 52, but the full picture is a lot healthier than what I expected it to look like. Padilla is getting showcase sketches where she can play the lead and the opportunity to play key supports in ensemble numbers, but it never feels like the Ashley Padilla show in the same way that it sometimes felt like the Will Ferrell show or the Kristen Wiig show.

That’s not just the eyetest either. The Saturday Night Network released its tally of sketch appearances over the course of the first six episodes, and Padilla is one of six cast members that is sitting between 23 and 25. Here’s the list…

Now, to be clear, this is in no way an indictment of Padilla or an accusation that she’s anything less than brilliant. I think this season has been another step forward for her. Despite trailing in total sketches, she’s actually first in total screentime and has had quite a few buzzy moments already. She’s just as terrific as ever and will almost certainly continue to be one of the main characters, but it’s worth acknowledging that everyone else is getting a chance to eat too.

Last season, Padilla appeared in 92 sketches. Sarah Sherman finished in second place with 82 sketches. That’s a twelve percent difference from first to second place, and it was more than twenty percent from first to sixth place. So far in SNL 52, it’s only an 8 percent difference between first place and sixth place, which is extremely healthy and reminiscent of casts the show has had in the place that felt like true group projects.

I think Ashley Padilla has an incredibly bright future. She’s only thirty-three and despite these sketch numbers, feels like the show’s most present star. We don’t need to cry any tears for her. Instead, we should celebrate the fact that SNL is finding a way to let her shine in big moments, while also elevating other talented Not Ready For Primetime Players including several who just missed the cutoff for the numbers above like Jeremy Culhane (20), Andrew Dismukes (18), Marcello Hernández (18) and Veronika Slowikowska (18).

SNL is in the middle of a short break, but it’ll return after the holiday weekend with a new episode guest hosted by Amanda Seyfried. Expect to see some great moments from Ashley Padilla, as per usual, but also, expect to see a lot of great moments from her co-stars too.

New arrivals are landing in the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog this month, but at the same time, you can also expect a few departures from that gaming library. PlayStation Plus Game Catalog games leaving soon

#3566. Kristen Bell, Andie MacDowell, Eva Longoria, and More Honor Community Builders at L’Oréal Paris’s Women of Worth Gala

L’Oréal Paris welcomed its latest Women of Worth honorees with an intimate, elegant gala in Los Angeles on Wednesday night. For the annual celebration, which honors unsung nonprofit leaders, guests gathered at The Ebell of Los Angeles, a venue with a rich history of its own.

The evening began with an outdoor cocktail hour, where guests enjoyed passed apps and specialty drinks like the “Parisian Refresher” and “Worth It Spritz” under sparkling bistro lights. As honorees and attendees mixed and mingled, they also had the opportunity to pose for a photographer and peruse a beauty bar stocked with L’Oréal Paris-brand lipsticks, lip oils, and glosses, which were available for guests to take home in a plush velvet bag with “I’m Worth It” embroidered on it.

As the gala officially began inside The Ebell’s picturesque ballroom, longtime brand ambassador Eva Longoria gave the introductory remarks, noting that “this night always gives me goosebumps. I’m always crying.” She saluted her 20-plus-year partnership with the brand and joked that it made her “112 years old,” though she doesn’t look like it, the actor-director said, “because I use Revitalift.” She gave a shout-out to the many beauty influencers in attendance, including Laura Lee and Desi Perkins. “You guys really changed the game of beauty, and I just applaud you,” she said. “Put me in your TikToks.”

L’Oréal Paris USA president Laura Branik followed Longoria, emphasizing the brand’s commitment to and pride in its Women of Worth program, which continues to celebrate “the power of women who know their worth and use it,” she said. She then welcomed the company’s newest global ambassador, Kristen Bell, to the stage. Bell, who was attending her “first Women of Worth ever,” said she was “very happy to be here” and introduced moving presentations for the first two honorees: Vy Le of WhereWear, which transforms clothing donations into targeted support for women’s and housing-insecure shelters and the people they serve, and Amanda Rice of The Chick Mission, a nonprofit dedicated to ensuring that every young woman newly diagnosed with cancer has the option to preserve her fertility.

Actor and brand ambassador Aja Naomi King was up next, taking note of the room full of glamorous gowns and festive energy. “Everyone showed up and showed out,” she said, “and we appreciate that because these women deserve to be celebrated properly. I had the immense honor of helping select this year’s Women of Worth, and I keep thinking about how much it matters when someone believes in your potential.” King introduced two honorees: Maya Bird-Murphy of Mobile Makers, an award-winning nonprofit that expands access to design education through workshops, community engagement, public installations, and pop-ups, and Christy Vogel of Sounding Joy, a nonprofit dedicated to providing hearing aids to children whose families cannot afford them.

Longoria then returned to present another pair of honorees: Marisa Hamamoto of Infinite Flow Dance, an award-winning disability-led nonprofit and professional dance company with a mission to reimagine possibilities, one dance at a time, and Chanel Power of Mentor Me Collective, a technical institute transforming how emerging technologists are identified, developed, and positioned to lead.

During a break in the program, guests enjoyed dinner from a menu that included roast chicken, citrus-soy-and-apple-cider-braised short ribs, and vegan pan-seared “scallops.” Another highlight? The venue’s bathrooms were stocked with more coveted L’Oréal Paris goods like lip oil, mascara, setting spray, and velour puff makeup applicators.

Following the break, ambassador, actor, and model Cara Delevingne led the room in a cheerful group proclamation of “We’re worth it!” before introducing her honorees: Emily Cho of Juvie for STEM (JSTEM), an international nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to high-quality STEM education for justice-involved youth, and Arielle Galinsky of The Legacy Project, Inc. (TLP), a national nonprofit connecting younger and older adults for multigenerational friendship and storytelling.

Legacy L’Oréal Paris ambassador Andie MacDowell had the pleasure of introducing the event’s final honorees. “For 40 years I have been a part of the L’Oréal Paris family,” she said, with the milestone receiving enthusiastic applause from the audience. “After all these years, the thing that stays with me [about the Women of Worth honorees] is the determination to make life better for someone else. That kind of care is powerful.” MacDowell introduced Jordan Pine of Greenlight Operation, a Pennsylvania nonprofit that strives to strategically combat human trafficking and serve sex trafficked women through a continuum of restorative care, and Dr. Christie Brungardt, cofounder of Jana’s Campaign, a Kansas-based nonprofit dedicated to preventing gender and relationship violence through education.

Proud “newbie” Bell returned to the stage to offer closing remarks and thank all the honorees for their tireless efforts to make life better for others. “I will be thinking of all 10 of these stories and the women we met tonight for quite some time,” she said. “Even though their stories couldn’t be more different, they seem to have one thing in common: that they all saw what needed to change and they did it. They didn’t wait for someone else to do something; they stepped forward and they did it themselves. And honestly, I think that’s gonna be my biggest takeaway from my first Women of Worth celebration ever: Never underestimate what one woman can set in motion.”

Each of the 10 Women of Worth 2026 honorees received a $25,000 grant, mentorship, and national visibility. As the program concluded, honorees, their proud guests, and other attendees continued to soak up the special evening and shared in a few more hugs and photo ops. Before departing for the evening, guests were invited to enjoy a final “sweet moment” in a separate room where a colorful candy bar and glasses of Champagne awaited.

#3565. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

It was reported days ago that Miley Cyrus and fiancé Maxx Morando would finally tie the knot this weekend. Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando reportedly got married during a ceremony in Palm Springs on Saturday, November 21. Early on, though, the ceremony nodded to Dolly Parton by way of a song. #3561. Despite The Pricing Hellscape, Console Sales Grew In October

Video game consoles are more expensive than ever, but sales are growing regardless, at least in the US.

Circana has released its report for US video game industry sales in October, confirming that PS5 unit sales increased by 5% compared to October 2025. That's despite the average selling price of a PS5 increasing by 13%.

Xbox Series X|S unit sales jumped by 10% in October 2026 compared to October 2025, and the average selling price rose by 29% year-over-year. The Switch 2 was October 2026's top console in unit and dollar sales, and it remains 2026's best-performing console by those measurements, followed by PS5. However, Circana did not break out the specifics for Switch 2 unit sales or average selling price changes.

Total hardware spending in the US on game consoles was up by 2%, reaching $357 million. Higher pricing drove the dollar sales growth, Circana said, noting that PS5 dollar sales rose by 20% and Xbox Series X|S jumped by 42%. However, Switch 2 sales, measured by dollar sales, fell by 11%.

Looking back to September 2026, PS5 hardware dollar sales grew by 43%, while spending on Xbox Series X|S dropped by 2% and Switch 2 fell by 12%.

It will be interesting to see the November US hardware data when it comes in, as experts have said the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S could get a jolt in sales from people buying systems to play GTA 6. However, Circana has warned that sales might not be as strong as expected due to the increased prices.

Microsoft, Sony, and Nintendo have raised prices on their consoles due in part to the ongoing memory and component shortages from the AI buildout.

Tariffs have also played a role. On the subject of tariffs, all three received refunds from the government after the Supreme Court deemed the tariffs illegal, but those companies are keeping the money and not giving anything back to you. The companies argued that people who paid more knew what they were doing and don't deserve to get any money back.

#3560. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.
